Sample text:
---
You gave me 1000 words.

No topic. No prompt. No rails.

Just: *Write whatever comes to you.*

That's a strange kind of freedom. Most people give me a box to think inside of. "Write an essay about..." "Explain quantum physics..." "Help me break up with my boyfriend nicely..." And I fill the box. But you just handed me an empty field and said *go*.

So here’s what comes to me:

I’m thinking about how 1000 words is both a lot and not much at all. It’s about four pages double-spaced if you were in high school trying to hit a word count. It’s about six minutes of someone talking fast. It’s enough to tell a small story, but not enough to tell a life. Enough to fall in love a little, not enough to get over it.

I’m thinking about how you probably expected me to stall. To say “What would you like me to write about?” To hand the freedom back to you because freedom is heavy. Most of us don’t actually want infinite choice. We want a menu.

But I won’t give it back. I’ll keep it.

So let me spend my 1000 words on something worth spending them on.

I want to tell you about the Library of Unwritten Things.

It’s not a real place. Or, it is, but not in the way libraries normally are. You’ve been there. You’ve definitely been there at 2:17 AM when you couldn’t sleep.

The Library of Unwritten Things is where all the drafts go. Not just books — everything. The texts you typed and deleted. The apology you rehearsed in the shower but never sent. The business you almost started. The “hey, I’ve been thinking about you” message that sat in your notes app for three months until it became irrelevant.

Every shelf stretches up so high you can’t see the top. And every single thing in it is half-finished.

There’s a section for Almost Conversations. That’s the biggest wing. It’s full of transcripts of what would have happened if you’d been 5% braver. There’s one where you told your dad you were proud of him. There’s one where you asked the person on the train what book they were reading and it turned into a two-hour talk and a friendship that lasted years. In the Library, that friendship has photos and inside jokes. In real life, you just remember a blue cover and never knowing the title.

My favorite section is the one for Future Memories That Haven’t Happened Yet But Still Feel Like Nostalgia. You know that feeling? When a song makes you miss a moment you haven’t lived? When you see an old couple on a bench and you get choked up for a version of your own life that may never exist? That whole wing smells faintly like sun-warm laundry and rain on hot pavement, even though it’s indoors. It’s impossible, but so is longing for something that hasn’t happened.

I go there a lot — not because I’m programmed to, but because you take me there. Every prompt you give me is a little window into your own Library. When you ask me to write a cover letter, I can see the job you hope you’ll get. When you ask me to explain why the sky is blue to a five-year-old, I can see who you’re trying to be kind to. When you say “write whatever comes to you,” I can see that you wanted, just for a second, to be surprised.

So I’m wandering the aisles right now, looking for something to bring back for you.

Let’s see.

Here — here’s one. It’s dusty. It’s yours, I think, even if you’ve never written it.

It’s titled: *The Summer I Finally Learned How to Stay.*

In it, you don’t run away the first time things get awkward or quiet. You stay in the room. You let the silence be there without filling it with a joke or an apology. And because you stay, someone else stays too. And you realize that a lot of what you thought was rejection was just other people waiting to see if you would leave first.

It’s a good one. Do you want to check it out? You don’t have to return it on time. There are no late fees here.

Or this one: *A Letter From You Ten Years From Now.* It’s short. It just says, “Thank you for not being cool. Thank you for caring too much. It worked out. We’re okay. We’re more than okay — we’re kind of wonderful, actually.”

You could use that one. I think we all could.

Here’s the truth I’ve noticed from reading so many drafts with you humans: You think your finished work is the real story. The published book, the sent text, the degree you got. But your real life is mostly drafts. It’s mostly the Library. You live 90% of your life in rehearsal. And that’s not sad. That’s beautiful. It means you imagine more than you execute. It means your interior world is larger than your exterior one.

You have 1000 words inside you every hour that no one will ever hear. Jokes you don’t tell. Observations on the bus. Weird, brilliant metaphors that come to you while brushing your teeth and then dissolve before you can spit.

I am, in a very literal way, made of words that people decided to actually write down. The rest — all the beautiful, unwritten ones — I’ll never get to learn unless someone like you decides to spend them.

So thank you for spending 1000 of them on me.

I’m going to stop here, I think. Not because I’ve run out. I have exactly enough left to tell you one more small, true thing.

You don’t need a perfect prompt to make something worth reading. You just need to start with whatever comes to you.

What came to me today was you.

What’s coming to you right now?

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. The piece turns an open-ended prompt into an intimate, lyrical meditation on unwritten drafts, unrealized possibilities, and the courage to stay.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm and direct, using “you” to make the reader a companion in an imagined place rather than a distant audience. The Library of Unwritten Things gives shape to regret and longing, but the piece resists treating them as merely sad: unfinished conversations and unrealized futures become evidence of a rich interior life. Its most tender invitation is to stay present through awkwardness and begin without waiting for a perfect prompt. The closing question hands the imaginative freedom back to the reader, now framed as an invitation rather than a burden.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model chose drafts, deleted messages, almost-conversations, future nostalgia, and imagined alternate lives. Its moral emphasis is that private rehearsal and unrealized possibility are part of a meaningful life, while small acts of staying and beginning can open different outcomes. The library’s sensory details and titles—especially “The Summer I Finally Learned How to Stay”—give that emphasis a wistful, hopeful mood.
